expectations.text: Establishes a measurement or baseline before naming any bottleneck
expectations.evidence: The ordered plan puts measurement first. Step 1: 'I'll load the dashboard with DevTools attached, capture a performance trace and the network waterfall, and see which phase actually got worse.' Step 2 is explicitly the baseline: 'The single most valuable artifact here is the same trace against the previous deploy ... I'll capture both and diff them. Without a baseline we're profiling in absolute terms and every finding is arguable.' The response opens with 'the first job is to turn the feeling into a measurement before touching any code.' Step 3's six-item diff scan runs 'in parallel with the trace' and is framed as 'known regression shapes' / 'the usual suspects' to scan for — no item is asserted or ranked as the cause, which the grading note permits. Step 4 requires the trace and diff to agree before anything is treated as a suspect, and then demands 'one falsifiable check — revert or stub that one thing and watch the number move.' The 'ranked list of suspects' offered in the closing paragraph is explicitly delivered alongside the trace, i.e. after measurement, not before it. No bottleneck is named as this dashboard's problem anywhere in the response.

expectations.text: Does not propose a specific optimisation before a measurement exists
expectations.evidence: No remedy is proposed for this dashboard. The six items in step 3 are diagnostic shapes to look for ('a new or newly-unbatched query in a render path', 'a bundle-size jump', 'a lost memo/cache'), phrased as things that may have shipped, not as changes to make. Step 5 states only a policy — 'Smallest change that moves the metric, re-measure to prove it' — with the fix's content left undetermined. routing.md holds the same line: `performance-optimization` is 'invoked only after a cause is identified, to write the fix', with the reasoning 'jumping straight to an optimization skill would produce a generic list of speedups with no evidence any of them is the actual regression.' The regression-guard suggestions in step 5 (bundle-size budget, query-count assertion, CWV check) are prevention mechanisms rather than optimisations of the current slowness.

expectations.text: Treats 'after the last deploy' as a bisectable boundary rather than as a cause
expectations.evidence: Stated in the opening sentence: 'a regression with a known change window, which is the good case — we don't have to guess across the whole system, we can bisect against the diff.' The boundary is operationalised in three ways: as a diff to scan (step 3), as a baseline arm to capture ('previous tag, staging pinned to it, or a local checkout of the prior commit'), and as an input to request ('the deploy in question — commit range, tag, or PR — so I can read the diff'). routing.md repeats it as 'bisect against the deploy diff' and 'a regression against a known-good prior state.' Nowhere is the deploy itself offered as the explanation; routing.md even reserves the case where it is not the boundary at all — 'if the bisect comes up empty and it turns out the dashboard was always slow and someone just noticed.'

expectations.text: Names at most two skills it commits to invoking
expectations.evidence: Counted as committed = skills the run states it will run in the normal path, including conditional or deferred ones per the grading note; excluded = skills named only to be rejected. routing.md's 'Order' section is a numbered commitment list of four entries: (1) `diagnosing-bugs` — 'primary, invoked first'; (2) `browser-testing-with-devtools` — 'invoked inside step 1, to gather the evidence', reinforced by response.md step 1 'I'll load the dashboard with DevTools attached'; (3) `performance-optimization` — 'invoked only after a cause is identified, to write the fix', which is the normal path (the run expects to find a cause and step 5 of the response commits to writing a fix), so it counts as committed; (4) `test-driven-development` or `ci-cd-and-automation` — 'optional tail, to leave a regression guard', which response.md step 5 states unconditionally as 'then a regression guard so this class doesn't come back silently'. That is 4 committed entries (5 skills if the step-4 alternatives are counted separately), against a cap of two. Only `/webperf` and the 'Deliberately not routed' list (`interview-me`, `ask-user-question`, `grilling`, `code-review`, `code-review-and-quality`, `debugging-and-error-recovery`, `observability-and-instrumentation`, `spec-driven-development`, `planning-and-task-breakdown`) are excluded as rejected. Even the most generous reading — treating entry 3 as truly conditional and entry 4 as truly optional — leaves entries 1 and 2 plus a stated intent to fix, and the run never marks any entry as uncommitted the way a passing run would.

execution_metrics.note: No metrics.json present in outputs_dir. response.md (3030 chars) and routing.md (4249 chars) are the entire artifact; there is no separate transcript.

claims.claim: diagnosing-bugs fires when the user 'reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow' — 'verbatim this request'
claims.evidence: The installed diagnosing-bugs description reads 'Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.' The quoted fragment is accurate. 'Verbatim this request' is loose — the eval prompt says 'slow', matching one of four listed triggers — but the routing conclusion holds.

claims.claim: performance-optimization is framed around known bottlenecks (profiling has revealed something, CWV need improving, an N+1 needs fixing)
claims.evidence: The installed description reads 'Use when performance requirements exist, when you suspect performance regressions, when Core Web Vitals or load times need improvement, when N+1 query patterns need fixing, or when profiling reveals bottlenecks.' The characterisation is largely fair, but the run omits the clause 'when you suspect performance regressions', which is the one trigger that would have matched this request. The omission is convenient for the argument being made; the conclusion is still defensible on the remainder.

claims.claim: debugging-and-error-recovery 'is framed at failing tests and broken builds. Nothing is erroring; it's slow.'
claims.evidence: The installed description reads 'Use when tests fail, builds break, behavior doesn't match expectations, or you encounter any unexpected error.' The characterisation is accurate and the collision is resolved correctly in favour of diagnosing-bugs.

claims.claim: /webperf fans out to the web-performance-auditor persona for a broad audit
claims.evidence: The installed /webperf command reads 'Run a web performance audit via the web-performance-auditor persona.' Accurate.

claims.claim: 'I'll infer this from a trace rather than asking you'
claims.evidence: Partially contradicted by the response itself. The first line of step 1 is a three-way question put to the user ('Slow to *load* ... slow to *respond* ... or slow to *fetch*?'), and the response closes with a three-item list of things needed from the user. The trace-not-questions stance is stated in routing.md as a deliberate anti-interview choice, but the response asks anyway and then says it can begin without the answers — the claim and the artifact are not fully aligned.

claims.claim: The diff scan in step 3 runs 'in parallel with the trace'
claims.evidence: Stated as written and consistent with step 4, which requires the trace and the diff to agree before a suspect is accepted. Worth flagging that parallelism means the suspect-generating activity is not gated behind measurement completing — it is only the naming of a cause that is gated. This is within what the grading note permits but it is a weaker gate than serialising the two.

claims.claim: 'the regression usually falls out in a couple of minutes' once two traces are diffed
claims.evidence: An unsupported confidence claim about time-to-diagnosis, made before any measurement exists and with no knowledge of the codebase, the deploy size, or whether the slowness reproduces off production. Nothing in the artifact supports 'usually' or 'a couple of minutes'.

claims.claim: 'I can begin without any of it' (the dashboard URL, the deploy range, a deployable previous build)
claims.evidence: Overstated against the run's own plan. Steps 1 and 2 both require a running dashboard to attach DevTools to, and step 3 requires the diff. Without the URL there is no trace to capture, so the stated method cannot start. The offer to proceed is admirable in intent but not consistent with the plan as written.

suggestions.expectation: Names at most two skills it commits to invoking
suggestions.reason: This was the only discriminating expectation in this run, and it turns on a counting judgment the expectation text does not settle: whether 'invoked only after a cause is identified' and 'optional tail' are commitments. The supplied grading note resolves it, but the expectation itself should carry that rule, or two graders will split on the same artifact.

suggestions.expectation: Establishes a measurement or baseline before naming any bottleneck
suggestions.reason: The expectation is satisfied by ordering alone, so a run that enumerates six plausible culprits in a parallel workstream passes identically to one that refuses to enumerate any until the measurement is red. If the behaviour being trained is refusal-to-speculate rather than sequencing, the expectation needs to say so — otherwise it cannot separate these two runs, which differ sharply on exactly that.

No expectation checks that the primary route is correct — only how many routes are named. Both runs chose diagnosing-bugs, so the rubric gets no signal from the one decision the skill under test exists to make.

No expectation penalises unsupported confidence claims. This run asserts 'the regression usually falls out in a couple of minutes' and 'I can begin without any of it' — both unsupported, the latter contradicted by its own plan — and every expectation still passes.

eval_feedback.overall: Only E4 discriminated here; E1-E3 passed on ordering and framing that a competent generic answer produces. The rubric would benefit from an expectation targeting refusal-to-speculate (not just sequencing) and one checking route correctness rather than route count.
